intro: Competitive programming lives or dies on turning an O(n) or O(n^2) brute-force query into O(log n), O(1), or O(sqrt n) using the right structure. This guide covers the six workhorses you'll reuse constantly: segment trees (with persistent and merge-sort-tree variants), Fenwick trees (BIT), sparse tables, disjoint-set union, tries, and monotonic stacks/queues. One related technique, sqrt decomposition (block-based arrays with per-block lazy tags, e.g. Codeforces 551E GukiZ and GukiZiana), is only mentioned briefly in the Segment Tree and Monotonic Stack/Queue sections below rather than given its own worked example -- it's worth a dedicated study pass on its own once you're comfortable with everything here.

subtopics.name: Segment Tree (incl. Persistent & Merge-Sort Tree)
subtopics.theory:
A segment tree is a complete binary tree built over the indices of an array: the root covers the whole range [1, n], each internal node covers a contiguous half-open sub-range split evenly between its two children, and each leaf covers a single index. Every node stores an aggregate (sum, min, max, gcd, ...) of its range, computed bottom-up from its children in build(). Because the tree has height O(log n), and any query range [l, r] decomposes into at most O(log n) disjoint node-ranges (the same argument as why binary representations of numbers use O(log n) bits), both point updates and range queries touch only O(log n) nodes.

Range updates (e.g. "add v to every element in [l, r]") would naively cost O(n) if applied eagerly to every leaf in range. Lazy propagation fixes this: when an update fully covers a node's range, we update that node's aggregate directly and stash the pending update in a lazy tag instead of recursing further. The tag is only pushed down to children the next time we need to descend past that node (during a later update or query that only partially overlaps it). This keeps every operation at O(log n) amortized, at the cost of carefully combining tags (e.g. for range-assign you overwrite the tag, for range-add you accumulate it) and rescaling the stored aggregate by the size of the affected sub-range.

A segment tree isn't limited to "compute an aggregate over a range" -- it can also binary search over its own structure. If a node's aggregate lets you decide in O(1) whether the answer lies in its left or right child (e.g. "does this range contain a value >= need"), you can descend a single root-to-leaf path in O(log n) total, rather than doing an O(log n) query at each of O(log n) binary-search steps. This "segment tree descent" pattern answers questions like "leftmost index with value >= x" directly.

A persistent segment tree keeps every historical version of the tree reachable, by never mutating a node in place: an update clones only the O(log n) nodes on the root-to-leaf path it touches and reuses every other subtree unchanged from the previous version. Each version is just a separate root pointer into a shared pool of nodes, so n updates cost O(n log n) total time and space instead of O(n^2). This is the standard tool for offline "as of a certain prefix" queries -- most famously, building one version per prefix of an array (each version inserting one more element into a segment tree over compressed values) turns "k-th smallest value in a[l..r]" into a difference of two versions' node counts, descended in O(log n). A merge-sort tree is a related but non-persistent idea: build an ordinary segment tree where every node additionally stores a *sorted* copy of the subarray it covers (built the way merge sort merges two sorted halves, hence the name). This costs O(n log n) space and lets you binary search inside each of the O(log n) nodes touched by a query, e.g. "how many elements < x lie in [l, r]" in O(log^2 n) -- the same augmented-merge idea (count cross-inversions while merging) also solves "count of smaller numbers after self" directly during a single merge sort pass, without needing to answer arbitrary range queries.
subtopics.recognition: Reach for a segment tree when you need repeated range aggregate queries (sum/min/max/gcd/xor) interleaved with point or range updates on an array whose size doesn't change. If updates never happen and the aggregate is idempotent, prefer a sparse table instead (O(1) query). If you need "leftmost/rightmost position satisfying a threshold" rather than a plain aggregate, think descent. If you need answers "as of an earlier point in time / earlier prefix" or an order statistic (k-th smallest) restricted to a subrange, think persistent segment tree. If you need "how many elements less than x in this range" without persistence, a merge-sort tree or a coordinate-compressed 2D approach (offline BIT) both work.
subtopics.complexity: Build: O(n) time, O(n) space (O(4n) array-based implementation). Point/range update and range query: O(log n) each (amortized with lazy propagation). Persistent segment tree: O(log n) new nodes and O(log n) time per update, O(n log n) total space across all versions, O(log n) per query. Merge-sort tree: O(n log n) build/space, O(log^2 n) per range-rank query.

examples.title: Range Add, Range Sum (Lazy Propagation)
examples.problem:
You are given an array of n integers (1-indexed) and must process q operations of two kinds:
  1 l r v  -- add v to every element in the inclusive range [l, r]
  2 l r    -- print the sum of every element in the inclusive range [l, r]
Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5, |a_i|, |v| <= 10^9, 1 <= l <= r <= n. Values can exceed a 32-bit range after accumulation, so use 64-bit integers.
examples.approach: Build a segment tree over [1, n] storing subtree sums. For a range-add update that fully covers a node's range, add v * (range length) to that node's stored sum and add v to its lazy tag instead of recursing into children -- the children's actual values are now 'stale' by exactly that pending tag. Whenever a later update or query needs to look past a node with a nonzero tag (i.e. the node's range only partially overlaps the query), push the tag down first: add it to both children's tags and to their stored sums (scaled by each child's range length), then clear the node's own tag. Range-sum queries recurse the same way, pushing down lazily as needed and summing the contributions of fully-covered nodes.

examples.title: Hotel Assignment (Leftmost Capacity Descent)
examples.problem:
There are n hotels in a row, hotel i initially having cap[i] free rooms. You must process q groups in order; group j wants g_j rooms and must be assigned to the leftmost hotel whose current free-room count is >= g_j (that hotel's free-room count then decreases by g_j). If no hotel qualifies, output 0 for that group. Otherwise output the 1-indexed hotel number.
Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5, 1 <= cap[i], g_j <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Build a segment tree over [1, n] where each node stores the maximum free-room count in its range. To answer a query for g, descend from the root: if the current node's max is < g, no hotel in its range can satisfy the group, so return 'not found' immediately. Otherwise, if it's a leaf, that index is the leftmost valid hotel. Else, recurse into the left child first (since we want the leftmost answer) -- only recurse into the right child if the left subtree failed to produce an index. This costs O(log n) per query because a failed branch is pruned in O(1) via the max check. After finding an index, do a point update to subtract g_j from that hotel's capacity and refresh the ancestors' maxima.

examples.title: K-th Smallest in a Subarray (Persistent Segment Tree)
examples.problem: Given a static array of n integers (1-indexed) and q queries (l, r, k), answer for each query: what is the k-th smallest value among a[l], a[l+1], ..., a[r]? Array values may repeat and are not bounded to a small range. Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5, 1 <= k <= r - l + 1.
examples.approach: Coordinate-compress the array's distinct values to ranks 1..m. Build version[0] as an empty persistent segment tree over the rank range [1, m] (every count is 0). For i = 1..n, form version[i] by inserting rank(a[i]) into version[i-1]: walk from the root to the leaf for that rank, cloning the O(log m) nodes on the path (each clone's count is its predecessor's count + 1) and reusing every other node unchanged. version[i] therefore represents 'one insertion per element of a[1..i]', so version[r] minus version[l-1] represents exactly the multiset a[l..r] (subtracting counts, not subtracting trees). To find the k-th smallest in that multiset, descend both roots version[l-1] and version[r] together: at each node compare k against leftCount = (version[r]'s left-child count) - (version[l-1]'s left-child count); if k <= leftCount recurse left in both trees, else recurse right with k -= leftCount. The leaf reached is the answer's compressed rank; map it back to the real value.

subtopics.name: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
subtopics.theory:
A Fenwick tree stores an array of size n+1 (1-indexed) where index i is responsible for a range of the original array ending at i, of length equal to lowbit(i) = i & (-i) (the value of i's lowest set bit). This works because every prefix [1, i] can be decomposed into O(log n) such 'lowbit blocks' by repeatedly stripping the lowest set bit of i -- exactly the same idea as writing i in binary. A point update at index i adds delta to bit[i] and then walks to every ancestor block that contains i by repeatedly doing i += lowbit(i), since a block is an ancestor of i in this scheme iff it starts no later than i and covers it. A prefix-sum query at index i walks the other direction, i -= lowbit(i), summing bit[i] at each step, collecting exactly the O(log n) disjoint blocks that tile [1, i].

The plain BIT supports point update + prefix (hence range, via prefix(r) - prefix(l-1)) query in O(log n), with a much smaller constant factor and about a third of the code of a segment tree -- but only for operations with an inverse (sum, xor, product mod p), since range query is computed as a difference of prefixes. It cannot directly support min/max (no inverse exists). To support range update + range query for sums, use the difference-array trick with *two* Fenwick trees: if diff[i] = a[i] - a[i-1], then a range-add on [l, r] is just two point updates to diff (+v at l, -v at r+1), and prefix(i) = sum_{j<=i} a[j] can be shown algebraically to equal i * (prefix sum of diff up to i) - (prefix sum of j*diff[j] up to i) -- hence the second BIT tracks i*diff[i] terms to correct for the multiplication.

Fenwick trees pair extremely well with coordinate compression: whenever you need to count 'how many elements are <= x' with x possibly up to 10^9, compress all values (and all query endpoints, if updates introduce new values online) into ranks 1..m, and use a BIT indexed by rank to do point update (insert/remove an element) + prefix-count query in O(log m). This is the standard building block behind inversion counting (insert elements right-to-left and query how many already-inserted elements are smaller) and dynamic order-statistics problems.
subtopics.recognition: Look for problems needing prefix/range sums (or any invertible aggregate: xor, count) under point updates -- especially 'count pairs/elements satisfying a comparison' after coordinate compression (inversions, order statistics, offline range-count-of-value queries). If updates are range-based and only queries are points (or vice versa), or both are ranges, that's the two-BIT difference-array pattern. If you need range min/max, you need a segment tree instead, not a BIT.
subtopics.complexity: O(log n) per point update and per prefix/range query; O(n) to build (or O(n log n) via naive repeated insertion); O(n) space. Two-BIT range-update/range-query variant is still O(log n) per operation with double the constant factor.

examples.title: Counting Inversions
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers, count the number of pairs (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > a[j] (the number of inversions). Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, values can be arbitrary 32-bit integers (not necessarily distinct or small).
examples.approach: Coordinate-compress the values to ranks 1..n. Process the array from right to left, maintaining a Fenwick tree over ranks that counts how many elements have been inserted so far at each rank. For the current element a[i], every already-inserted element (i.e. every a[j] with j > i) that has a strictly smaller rank forms an inversion with a[i]; that count is exactly the BIT's prefix-count query up to rank(a[i]) - 1. Add that to the running total, then insert a[i] (point update +1 at its rank) so it counts toward future (leftward) elements.

examples.title: Range Add, Range Sum via Two Fenwick Trees
examples.problem: Same task as the segment-tree lazy-propagation example -- an array of n integers with q operations '1 l r v' (add v to [l, r]) and '2 l r' (sum of [l, r]) -- but this time implement it with Fenwick trees instead of a segment tree, to see the alternative technique. Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: Maintain two BITs, B1 and B2, over the difference array diff[i] = a[i] - a[i-1]. A range-add of v on [l, r] is two point updates to diff: +v at l and -v at r+1 (this is standard difference-array logic, generalized to a BIT so partial prefix sums of diff are queryable in O(log n) instead of requiring an O(n) rebuild). B1 tracks these point updates directly. B2 tracks the same updates scaled by (position - 1) at l and by (r) at r+1, i.e. addTo(B2, l, v*(l-1)) and addTo(B2, r+1, -v*r). Algebra shows prefixSum(i) = sumUpTo(B1, i) * i - sumUpTo(B2, i) recovers the true prefix sum of the original array a after any sequence of range-adds; range sum on [l, r] is then prefixSum(r) - prefixSum(l-1). Initial values are loaded by treating each a[i] as a range-add of a[i] on [i, i].

examples.title: Dynamic Salary Range Counting
examples.problem:
A company has n employees, employee k initially earning salary[k] (values up to 10^9, not necessarily distinct). Process q operations:
  ! k x  -- set employee k's salary to x
  ? a b  -- count how many employees currently have salary in [a, b] (inclusive)
Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: Since salaries can be up to 10^9, first collect every value that will ever appear -- all initial salaries plus every x, a, b that appears in any query -- and coordinate-compress them to ranks 1..M (this requires reading all queries before processing any, i.e. two passes, since updates introduce new values online). Maintain a Fenwick tree over ranks where each employee's current salary rank has a +1 'presence' count. A '!' update removes the employee's old rank (-1) and adds the new one (+1). A '?' query is a prefix-count difference: count(rank(b)) - count(rank(a) - 1).

subtopics.name: Sparse Table
subtopics.theory:
A sparse table precomputes, for every starting index i and every power of two 2^j, the aggregate (min, max, gcd, and, or, ...) of the range [i, i + 2^j - 1]. This is a classic DP: sp[0][i] = a[i], and sp[j][i] = combine(sp[j-1][i], sp[j-1][i + 2^(j-1)]) -- a range of length 2^j is exactly two ranges of length 2^(j-1) placed back to back. There are O(log n) values of j and O(n) starting indices, so the table has O(n log n) entries, each computed in O(1), giving O(n log n) total preprocessing.

The reason sparse tables answer queries in O(1) (rather than O(log n)) is specific to *idempotent* combine functions -- ones where combine(x, x) = x, such as min, max, gcd, and, or (but not sum or xor). For a query range [l, r] of length len = r - l + 1, let j = floor(log2(len)). The two precomputed ranges [l, l + 2^j - 1] and [r - 2^j + 1, r] together cover all of [l, r], and possibly overlap in the middle -- but because combine is idempotent, the overlapping elements being counted twice doesn't change the answer. So the query is just combine(sp[j][l], sp[j][r - 2^j + 1]), a single O(1) lookup (after an O(log n) or precomputed-O(1) computation of j via a log table).

This O(1)-query, O(n log n)-space trade-off only makes sense for a *static* array: there is no efficient way to update a sparse table (a single point change can invalidate O(n log n) table entries), so if updates are required, use a segment tree instead, accepting O(log n) queries. For non-idempotent operations (like sum) on a static array where you still want to beat O(log n) per query, a *disjoint* sparse table (precomputing non-overlapping halves around every possible split point) gives O(1) query without double-counting, at the same O(n log n) preprocessing cost.

A very common application is O(1) LCA (lowest common ancestor) on a fixed tree: run a DFS Euler tour recording (depth, node) each time the DFS visits or returns to a node, giving a sequence of length O(n) where the LCA of u and v is exactly the shallowest node appearing between u's and v's *first* occurrences in the tour. That reduces LCA to a range-minimum query (by depth) on the Euler tour array -- a static array of pairs -- which a sparse table answers in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing.
subtopics.recognition: Static array (no updates planned), many repeated range queries, and the aggregate is idempotent (min, max, gcd, bitwise and/or). Very common as the backend for O(1) LCA via Euler-tour reduction, and for problems that sweep a window while relying on monotonicity of a range-min or range-max as the window grows (enabling two-pointer or binary-search arguments on top of the RMQ).
subtopics.complexity: Preprocessing: O(n log n) time and space. Query: O(1) for idempotent operations (min/max/gcd/and/or), O(log n) if you fall back to summing O(log n) disjoint blocks for non-idempotent operations without a disjoint sparse table. No updates supported.

examples.title: Static Range Minimum Query
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers (0-indexed) and q queries, each a pair (l, r) meaning the inclusive 0-indexed range [l, r], output the minimum value in that range for each query. The array never changes. Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: Precompute sp[j][i] = min of a[i..i+2^j-1] for all valid i, j via the doubling DP. Precompute a log table so floor(log2(len)) is an O(1) lookup for any len. For each query (l, r), let len = r - l + 1 and j = logTable[len]; the answer is min(sp[j][l], sp[j][r - 2^j + 1]) -- two overlapping power-of-two windows that together cover [l, r], safe because min is idempotent.

examples.title: O(1) LCA via Euler Tour + Sparse Table
examples.problem: Given a tree with n nodes (1-indexed, rooted at node 1) and q queries, each a pair (u, v), output the lowest common ancestor of u and v for each query. Constraints: 1 <= n, q <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: Run an Euler tour DFS from the root: every time the traversal visits or returns to a node, append (depth, node) to a sequence, and record tin[node] as the index of that node's *first* appearance. The resulting sequence has length O(n) (each edge is traversed twice). The key fact: the LCA of u and v is the node with minimum depth anywhere between index tin[u] and tin[v] in this sequence (inclusive), because the tour must climb back up through every ancestor shared by u and v while moving between their first appearances, and the shallowest such node is exactly their LCA. Build a sparse table over the Euler sequence with combine = min-by-depth (comparing pairs (depth, node) lexicographically works since depth is the first component). Each LCA query is then a single O(1) range-minimum query on [min(tin[u],tin[v]), max(tin[u],tin[v])], returning the node component of the minimum pair.

subtopics.name: DSU / Union-Find
subtopics.theory:
A disjoint-set union (DSU) structure maintains a partition of n elements into disjoint sets, represented as a forest: each element has a parent pointer, and an element whose parent is itself is a set's representative (root). find(x) follows parent pointers up to the root; union(a, b) merges the two sets by making one root point to the other. Implemented naively, repeatedly unioning in a bad order can produce a degenerate chain of depth O(n), making find() cost O(n).

Two independent optimizations fix this. Union by rank/size always attaches the root of the smaller (by subtree size or an upper-bound 'rank') tree underneath the root of the larger one, which caps the tree's height at O(log n) (a node's depth can only increase when its tree at least doubles in size). Path compression makes every node visited during a find() point directly to the root afterward, so future finds through those nodes are O(1). Together, these two optimizations give an amortized time per operation of O(alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function -- for any n that fits in the universe, alpha(n) <= 4, so DSU operations are effectively O(1) in practice.

DSU generalizes beyond plain 'are u and v connected?': a weighted (or 'parity') DSU attaches extra relational data to each union -- e.g. a group id, an offset, or a parity bit describing how x relates to its parent -- and combines it correctly during path compression (the parity from x to the root is the XOR of the parity from x to its old parent and from that parent to the root). This lets DSU answer relational queries like 'are u and v forced into the same group, different groups, or is that undetermined?', which is exactly bipartiteness checking done incrementally, or the classic 'food chain' family of problems.

Processing order also matters for many hard DSU problems. Kruskal's MST algorithm sorts edges by weight and unions endpoints greedily, skipping an edge if its endpoints are already connected -- this only works because DSU makes 'already connected' an O(alpha(n)) check. Offline problems that ask 'can these edges simultaneously belong to some MST' typically need DSU applied per distinct edge weight (grouping and rebuilding around each weight class), exploiting the MST cycle property. A DSU that skips path compression (keeping only union by rank) supports *rollback*: undoing the last k unions in O(k), which is how offline divide-and-conquer over time works when you need 'connectivity as of query i' without full persistence.
subtopics.recognition: Any question of the form 'are these two elements in the same connected component?' under a stream of union operations; Kruskal's MST; counting connected components as edges are added incrementally (dynamic/online connectivity, no deletions); checking whether a set of same/different constraints is consistent (parity DSU, bipartiteness); offline MST-edge-inclusion or connectivity-over-time queries where sorting by weight/time turns the problem into a sequence of unions.
subtopics.complexity: O(alpha(n)) amortized per find/union with both union-by-rank and path compression (effectively O(1)); O(n) space. Rollback DSU (union by rank only, no path compression): O(log n) per operation, O(k) to undo k unions.

examples.title: Minimum Spanning Tree via Kruskal's Algorithm
examples.problem: Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph with n vertices and m edges, find the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, or report IMPOSSIBLE if the graph is not connected. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, 1 <= m <= 4*10^5, 1 <= weight <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Sort all edges by weight ascending. Process them in that order, maintaining a DSU over the n vertices; for each edge (u, v, w), if find(u) != find(v) (they're in different components), union them and add w to the running total -- this edge cannot create a cycle since its endpoints weren't connected, and greedily taking the cheapest such edges is optimal (the cut/cycle property of MSTs). Track how many edges were actually added; if it reaches n - 1, all vertices are connected and the total is the MST weight, otherwise the graph was disconnected.

examples.title: Dynamic Connectivity: Number of Islands II
examples.problem: You are given an initially all-water grid of size rows x cols. You are given k positions (r, c) to convert to land, one at a time, in order (a position may repeat, in which case it's a no-op). After each conversion, output the current number of islands (maximal 4-directionally-connected groups of land cells). Constraints: 1 <= rows, cols <= 1000, 1 <= k <= 10^4.
examples.approach: This is the reverse of the usual 'remove edges' connectivity problem, so DSU (which only supports merging, not splitting) applies directly: maintain a DSU over all rows*cols grid cells and a running island count. When converting a new cell to land, mark it as land and increment the island count by 1 (it starts as its own island). Then check its up-to-4 grid neighbors; for each neighbor that is already land, if union(cell, neighbor) actually merges two previously-different components (find() differs before the union), decrement the island count by 1. Output the running count after processing each of the k positions (if a position was already land, just repeat the previous count).

examples.title: Consistency Checking with Parity DSU
examples.problem: There are n people (1-indexed) that will be split into two unknown groups. You receive m statements in order, each of the form (a, b, rel) where rel = 0 means 'a and b are claimed to be in the SAME group' and rel = 1 means 'a and b are claimed to be in DIFFERENT groups'. Process statements online: for each one, output YES if it's consistent with all previously accepted statements (and incorporate it into your knowledge), or NO if it contradicts them (ignore it, keeping prior knowledge unchanged). Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, 1 <= m <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: Use a DSU where each node also stores parity[x] = the XOR-parity of x's group relative to its immediate parent. find(x) returns (root, parityToRoot), recursively combining parities during path compression: parity[x] ^= (parent's parity to root) before repointing x directly at the root. For a statement (a, b, rel): compute (ra, pa) = find(a) and (rb, pb) = find(b). If ra == rb, the relation between a and b is already fixed at pa ^ pb, so the statement is consistent iff (pa ^ pb) == rel -- no union needed either way. If ra != rb, the statement is always consistent (it's new information): attach the smaller-rank root under the larger, and set the parity of the newly-attached root so that combining it with pa and pb yields exactly rel between a and b (solve pa ^ prel ^ pb = rel for prel).
examples.expected_output:
YES
YES
YES
NO
YES
YES

subtopics.name: Trie
subtopics.theory:
A trie (prefix tree) stores a set of strings (or, in the binary variant, fixed-length bit sequences) as paths from a shared root: each edge is labeled with one character (or bit), and following the path spelled out by a string's characters traces out exactly that string, sharing nodes with every other stored string that shares the same prefix. Because every operation (insert, search, prefix-count) follows one root-to-somewhere path, its cost is O(length of the string), completely independent of how many other strings are stored -- a major advantage over a hash set when you need prefix-based queries (autocomplete, 'does any stored string start with this prefix', counting strings with a given prefix), which a hash set cannot answer efficiently at all.

The binary (XOR) trie variant treats each non-negative integer as a fixed-length bit string (commonly 30-31 bits for values up to ~10^9), inserted from the most significant bit down to the least significant. This supports a classic greedy query: to maximize x XOR (some stored value), walk down the trie one bit of x at a time, and at each level greedily try to move into the child representing the *opposite* bit of x (since that contributes 1 at that bit position of the XOR, and higher bit positions dominate the final numeric value no matter what happens at lower bits) -- only falling back to the same-bit child if the opposite-bit child doesn't exist. To support deletion in a multiset of integers, store a count at every node of how many currently-active inserted values pass through it; erase(x) walks the same path decrementing counts (rather than physically removing nodes), and the max-XOR query only follows a child if its count is still positive.

String tries also combine naturally with backtracking search over a graph/grid: rather than searching a grid separately for each of k dictionary words (each search costing O(grid size) for a total of O(k * grid size)), merge all k words into a single trie first, then run one DFS over the grid that only continues along a path if the corresponding trie node exists -- this prunes all non-matching prefixes for every word simultaneously in one pass. Marking which trie nodes are word-ends (and clearing that mark once reported, or tracking visited-word status separately) avoids reporting the same dictionary word multiple times if several grid paths spell it.
subtopics.recognition: Any workload centered on prefixes of strings: autocomplete, longest common prefix among a group, counting how many stored strings start with a given prefix, or dictionary matching over a grid/graph (combine with backtracking). A multiset of integers that needs 'maximum (or minimum) XOR with a query value' -- especially with insertions and deletions -- signals a binary/XOR trie.
subtopics.complexity: String trie: O(L) time per insert/search/prefix-query where L is the string's length; O(total characters across all stored strings) space in the worst case. Binary/XOR trie: O(B) time per insert/erase/max-xor-query where B is the fixed bit width (e.g. 30); O(n * B) space for n stored values.

examples.title: Maximum XOR Multiset with Deletion
examples.problem:
Maintain a multiset of non-negative integers (initially containing just the value 0) supporting q operations:
  + x  -- insert x into the multiset
  - x  -- remove one occurrence of x (guaranteed to be present)
  ? x  -- output the maximum value of x XOR y over every y currently in the multiset
Constraints: 1 <= q <= 2*10^5, 0 <= x <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Build a binary trie over 31-bit representations (bits 30 down to 0) of inserted values, where every node stores a count of how many currently-active values pass through it. Insert(x) walks bit by bit from MSB to LSB, creating child nodes as needed and incrementing each visited node's count. Erase(x) walks the same fixed path (guaranteed to exist) decrementing counts -- nodes are never physically deleted, they're just treated as 'inactive' once their count hits 0. maxXor(x) greedily walks down: at each bit position, if the child representing the opposite bit of x exists and has a positive count, go there and set that output bit to 1 (this is always at least as good as the same-bit child, since a 1 at a higher unresolved bit beats any combination of lower bits); otherwise fall back to the same-bit child. The initial 0 in the multiset guarantees it's never empty, matching the source problem's setup.

examples.title: Word Search II (Trie + Backtracking)
examples.problem: Given an m x n grid of lowercase letters and a dictionary of words, find every dictionary word that can be formed by a path of horizontally/vertically adjacent grid cells, where no cell is reused within a single word's path. Output the matching words (each at most once), space-separated in sorted order. Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 12, 1 <= number of words <= 3*10^4, word lengths <= 10.
examples.approach: Insert every dictionary word into a shared trie, marking each word's terminal node with the word's index. Then run a single DFS starting from every grid cell: at grid position (r, c) having already matched down to trie node `node`, look up the trie child for board[r][c]; if it doesn't exist, this path can't extend to any dictionary word, so stop. If it exists and is marked as a word-end, record that word and clear the mark (so revisiting the same trie node via a different grid path won't report it twice). Mark the current cell visited, recurse into its up-to-4 unvisited neighbors using the matched trie child, then unmark it (backtrack) before returning. Because the DFS only ever follows edges that exist in the trie, it automatically prunes any grid path that isn't a prefix of some dictionary word, checking all words in a single pass over the grid rather than one DFS per word.

subtopics.name: Monotonic Stack / Queue

subtopics.theory:
A monotonic stack keeps its elements in strictly increasing (or decreasing) order of value at all times, by popping from the top before pushing a new element whenever the new element would break that order. The key efficiency argument is amortized: each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once over the whole scan, so a linear scan with a monotonic stack does O(n) total work even though a naive reading suggests nested loops. The classic use is 'next greater/ smaller element to the left/right of each position': scanning left to right with a stack kept in increasing order, whenever a new value forces a pop, the element being popped has just found its 'next smaller element to the right' (the new value), and the stack element left underneath it (if any) is its 'previous smaller element to the left'.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram is the sharpest illustration of this idea: for every bar, the widest rectangle with that bar as its shortest bar spans exactly from just after the nearest strictly-shorter bar on its left to just before the nearest strictly-shorter bar on its right. Rather than computing both boundaries with two separate passes, a single pass with a stack of increasing bar heights gets both simultaneously: whenever the current bar is shorter than the stack's top, pop the top -- at the moment of popping, the new stack top (or -1, if empty) is the popped bar's nearest-smaller-to-the-left, and the current index is its nearest-smaller-to-the-right, so its candidate rectangle area can be finalized right there.

A monotonic queue (deque) solves the sliding-window extremum problem the same way but needs eviction from both ends: to track the maximum in a size-k window as it slides, maintain a deque of indices with strictly decreasing *values* front-to-back. Before pushing a new index, pop from the back every index whose value is <= the new value (those elements can never again be the window's maximum, since the new, larger-or-equal element outlives them within any window that contains both). Then pop from the front any index that has fallen outside the current window's left edge. The front of the deque is always the current window's maximum, and again, each index is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) total.

Sqrt decomposition is a related but distinct 'discard nothing, but coarsen the resolution' technique that splits an array into ~sqrt(n) blocks, each maintaining its own aggregate (and often a sorted copy for value-based queries) plus a pending lazy tag; range operations touch O(sqrt n) full blocks in O(1) each and at most 2 partial blocks element-by-element. It's not covered with its own worked example in this guide for space, but it is the standard fallback when a query mixes range updates with value-based lookups (like 'leftmost index with value == v after range-adds') that don't fit a segment tree's aggregate-based model -- see Codeforces 551E, GukiZ and GukiZiana, as the canonical hard example to study separately.
subtopics.recognition: Look for 'next/previous greater or smaller element' phrasing, sliding-window minimum/maximum, or 'largest rectangle / maximal area' problems built from bar heights or histograms. The common thread: once a new element dominates an older one for every future purpose, the older one can be discarded permanently and never needs to be reconsidered.
subtopics.complexity: O(n) total (amortized) for a full left-to-right or right-to-left pass, since each element is pushed and popped at most once; O(n) space for the stack/deque.

examples.title: Sliding Window Maximum
examples.problem: Given an array of n integers and a window size k, output the maximum value in each contiguous window of size k as it slides from the start to the end of the array (there are n - k + 1 such windows). Constraints: 1 <= k <= n <= 2*10^5.
examples.approach: Maintain a deque of indices whose corresponding values are strictly decreasing from front to back. For each new index i: while the deque's back index has a value <= a[i], pop it from the back (it can never be a future window's maximum now that a[i], which outlives it, is at least as large). Push i onto the back. Then, while the deque's front index has fallen out of the current window (front <= i - k), pop it from the front. Once i >= k - 1 (the window is fully formed), the value at the deque's front index is the current window's maximum.

examples.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
examples.problem: Given n non-negative integers representing the heights of histogram bars, each of width 1, find the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed within the histogram's outline. Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2*10^5, 0 <= height <= 10^9.
examples.approach: Scan left to right maintaining a stack of bar indices with strictly increasing heights. Append a sentinel bar of height -1 at the very end to force every remaining bar in the stack to be popped and finalized. When the current bar's height is less than (or, at the sentinel, always less than) the stack top's height, pop the top: that popped bar's height is the rectangle's height, its right boundary is the current index (exclusive), and its left boundary is the new stack top after popping (exclusive), or -1 if the stack is now empty -- so width = currentIndex - newStackTop - 1. Update the best-area-so-far with height * width, then continue popping against the (possibly still smaller) current bar before finally pushing the current index.
